stories.headline: Fernando Mendoza relishes 'once-in-a-lifetime' opportunity as Raiders' QB1
stories.summary: No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza said Wednesday it's a "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunity to be the Raiders' starting quarterback, while his teammates and coach expressed their confidence in his ability to lead the offense.
stories.body:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Thrust back into the spotlight after months as Kirk Cousins' understudy, No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza said Wednesday it's a "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunity to be the Las Vegas Raiders' starting quarterback.

Being the starter is a "new step" in his career, Mendoza said. Nonetheless, he's trying to avoid making the moment bigger than it has to be.

Mendoza's starting debut Sunday will come against the reigning Super Bowl champions and one of the league's most imposing defenses, the Seattle Seahawks.

Through his preparation and Cousins' mentorship since the spring, Mendoza is confident in his ability to run the offense and has gained the utmost trust from his teammates and coach Klint Kubiak.

"I'm a lot more confident as a quarterback and feel more developed, whether it's [playing] under center, connecting with teammates, understanding an NFL scheme," Mendoza said Wednesday. "There are so many areas that I have improved on, and I look forward to keep on improving."

Kubiak said this week shouldn't feel like a whirlwind for Mendoza because he has been preparing the right way from the beginning. Kubiak also said the Raiders will not be "peeling back anything" in their offense, as the coach is comfortable with Mendoza running the entire playbook.

"We're going to go do what the whole team does best, all 11, and then he does his part distributing the football," Kubiak said.

Mendoza's teammates understand the challenges of adjusting to the pro level and are rallying behind the 23-year-old signal-caller. Tight end Brock Bowers said he's "excited" for Mendoza's first start and can't wait to see him sling the ball around the field.

Bowers said Mendoza has a good challenge ahead of him, facing Seattle's defense that has given up the fewest total yards per game in the league (244.2) and is tied for fourth in points allowed per game (18).

"Everyone has faith in him," Bowers said. "[Mendoza] might have a bad play here and there, but you just got to flush it. I know he does a good job at that."

Raiders wide receiver Tre Tucker said there isn't anything Mendoza can't do and that he brings consistency, a trait Tucker likes to see from a quarterback.

Tucker said Wednesday's practice with Mendoza as QB1 went "great" and it was good to see Mendoza in a flow.

"We've been seeing it all year," Tucker said. "He's been taking reps with us. He's been doing everything, and you just see a throw in practice and say, 'Wow.' For that to be out there this Sunday is going to be fun."

Despite all the attention on Mendoza, Cousins' absence in the locker room has been clearly felt. The Raiders' decision to trade Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings left many surprised, including Mendoza, who was in the locker room when the news broke.

Mendoza said he had "no inkling" his mentor would be traded.

"People were like, 'Kirk got traded,' and everyone just said that's the nature of the business, and that's how it is," Mendoza said. "And I'm excited to see Kirk in his future."

Mendoza commended Cousins and his family for welcoming him with open arms. Cousins welcomed Mendoza into his household while in Las Vegas, was never dismissive and offered guidance without any conditions.

"Everyone [saw] the Netflix show and you hear things from media, but to actually be in with him and spend long hours just in the quarterback room with him was extremely special," Mendoza said. "I'm going to miss him, and I really appreciate and am deeply thankful for everything that the Cousins family has offered to me."

Raiders starting center Tyler Linderbaum said he was "absolutely" surprised by Cousins' departure. He said Cousins put himself in a position where teams wanted him, but Linderbaum wished that hadn't been the case.

Tucker said it was hard to see Cousins leave, calling him "one of the best human beings" he has ever met. But Tucker also said he knew the day was coming, which made it easier for him to handle the past 24 hours. Tucker said Cousins left the Raiders in a better place than he found them.

One of Tucker's best memories was seeing the dynamic between Cousins and Mendoza.

"How Kirk is now, that's how Fernando will be when he's Kirk's age," Tucker said. "They were great together."

stories.headline: Matvei Michkov didn't ask Flyers for trade, Rick Tocchet says
stories.summary: Flyers coach Rick Tocchet said Wednesday that winger Matvei Michkov has not asked the organization for a trade.
stories.body:
EDMONTON, Alberta -- Philadelphia Flyers coach Rick Tocchet said Wednesday that winger Matvei Michkov has not asked the organization for a trade.

Tocchet's comments ahead of a game at the Edmonton Oilers came in the aftermath of a report Tuesday saying Michkov would likely want a change of scenery.

"There's nothing to talk about because it's not true," Tocchet said. "There's nothing important. You can't comment on somebody blogging something that's not true."

Asked if he was happy in Philadelphia, Michkov said, "Yeah, of course." The young Russian, who leads the team with 10 goals and is tied for the most points with 14, said he does not read the news and is focused on games.

Coming off a surprise run to the second round of the playoffs, the Flyers have lost 15 of their first 20 games as the NHL season nears the quarter mark.

stories.headline: UFC's Josh Hokit says he'll 'never' regret vulgar Michelle Obama remarks
stories.summary: UFC fighter Josh Hokit, who will challenger for the heavyweight title on Saturday, says he'll "never" regret his vulgar comments about former First Lady Michelle Obama,
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- UFC heavyweight Josh Hokit said he has no regrets about using the White House as a bully pulpit to make an extraordinary and unfounded attack based on a right-wing conspiracy theory about former first lady Michelle Obama.

Hokit made his vulgar remarks inside the Octagon in June after winning his fight at the UFC event to mark President Donald Trump's 80th birthday on the South Lawn of the White House.

Hokit fights for the first time since then on Saturday when he challenges heavyweight champion Ciryl Gane in the main event of UFC 334 at Madison Square Garden.

Hokit again made a series of crass insults about other fighters on the fight card on Wednesday inside a New York hotel before taking questions about his championship bout and his remarks on Obama.

"I'll never look back and be like, I regret that," Hokit said.

Wearing a black stocking cap over an American flag bandana, sunglasses and fight gloves, Hokit said he "took the rap of a villain" before he burst into what he called a freestyle rap to express his lack of regret.

Hokit said he was "sure it wasn't" the right thing to do to insult the former first lady but was proud the remarks had put his image on Trump's Truth Social posts. In one post, Hokit appeared in cartoon form alongside UFC chief Dana White in the White House briefing room.

Trump said over the weekend he had offered White the job of White House press secretary. White declined the frivolous offer.

"I'm here to take what's mine," Hokit said. "If I've got to rub some people the wrong way, if I've got to say some (stuff) in the wrong location, it is what it is. Was it not a good location to say it? I mean, we're at the White House. That house represents freedom of speech. So it is what it is. I think it was the perfect location to say it."

The 28-year-old Hokit is 10-0 in his MMA career and has won all six fights since joining UFC in 2025.

stories.headline: Will MLS teams' regular-season momentum last the two weeks before the playoffs start?
stories.summary: The MLS regular season ended on Saturday, but it will be nearly two weeks before the playoffs begin. It's a long time for a hot team to cool off.
stories.body:
With MLS Cup playoffs approaching, one word that continually comes up is "momentum." Does a team have it? If so, how can it maintain it, especially against the league's better teams? If not, how can the team get it back?

That said, the postseason does plenty to wreck the very concept of momentum. The league's playoffs are as unpredictable as it gets. Brackets are routinely demolished.

Nobody knows better the fickle nature of momentum than former MLS player and current Apple TV broadcaster Dax McCarty. He was part of the 2013 Supporters' Shield-winning Red Bull New York side that was eliminated in the Eastern Conference semifinal by the Houston Dynamo, thanks in part to a red card in the first leg to standout defender Jamison Olave.

McCarty was also part of the 2024 Atlanta United side that squeaked into the playoffs on Decision Day, beat CF Montréal in the wild card and then sprung an incredible upset against the juggernaut that was that year's Inter Miami side in Round 1. The win over Miami was aided by Atlanta keeper Brad Guzan performing physics-defying feats of gymnastics in the Five Stripes' goal.

"If the playoffs have taught us anything over the course of Major League Soccer's existence, it's that [you should] throw all that stuff out the window at times," McCarty told ESPN. "Throw tactics out the window, throw out momentum, throw out form, because one crazy play, one red card, one fluky goal can be the difference between advancing or your season being over."

Yet momentum is something that is still prized by coaches. In a world of fine margins, if you believe that you're going to win because of how you're playing in the moment, then the chances are better that the form will continue.

"I think momentum always matters, whether it's going into the postseason or whether it's the second game of the season," Houston Dynamo manager Ben Olsen said. "I think it matters mostly just because you want your team peaking around playoff time, and being the best version of themselves."

San Jose Earthquakes boss Bruce Arena stressed that momentum is as much a state of mind as it is about results. That's especially true if a coach feels his team is still short of its best.

"It doesn't have to be a terrific run going into the playoffs, but you have to have a team going in with confidence," he said. "You need to have a pretty good idea about what your team's about and how you want to go about your business in the playoffs.

"Probably the psychological part of it is more important than actually the tactical part of it. You just got to get inside the team and make sure that they enter the game with the confidence that they can get a result."

That appears to be true for the Quakes, who finished the season by going 4W-7D-2L. Houston, who faces San Jose in the first round, went a more sobering 2W-7D-4L.

At this stage of the season, teams have already been together for 10 months, so a manager is bound to know what makes his team tick. That doesn't mean said manager's work is done. There could be collaborative meetings in terms of refining how the team wants to approach a certain opponent.

Individual meetings might be needed as well to bolster the confidence of a particular player. A lineup change or a subtle tactical tweak could help a team as well. Arena stressed there is no formula for how he handles things.

"I think I've been in seven MLS Cup finals and won five of them, and I don't think I can tell you that I had the same approach to any of them," Arena said. "Every one was different."

The issue of momentum -- whether trying to maintain it or generate it -- faces some tricky obstacles this postseason. Following last Saturday's Decision Day, the teams that qualified for the playoffs will get around two weeks between matches due to the FIFA international window.

With rhythm broken, the playing field would appear to be more level. That provokes myriad questions in terms of approach. McCarty said the break "absolutely" has an effect on rhythm, momentum and potential injuries.

"How hard do you push your players? You want your players in form, but you also don't want them to get injured," McCarty said. "How hard are the coaches going to push their players?"

There seem to be two paths a manager can take. They either have a scrimmage against another MLS team, or they have an intra-squad match, albeit one in a stadium with referees, the better to simulate a real match. There are pros and cons to both. With injury prevention paramount, playing against another MLS team would appear to offer less control on the level of physicality.

"I think you would want to keep it in-house in terms of an intra-squad scrimmage to try to keep your players fit, to try to keep your players sharp, and with the very real caveat before the game to say, 'Listen, there are no dumb tackles. There are no slide tackles,'" McCarty said. "If you are an Inter Miami fan or a New England Revolution fan or a Nashville SC fan, you're telling young players that might be involved, 'You are not allowed to touch Hany Mukhtar. You're not allowed to touch Carles Gil. You're not allowed to touch [Lionel] Messi.'

"Those are the very clear expectations you have to set. But guess what? That doesn't actually give you a realistic playoff feel. It's whoever can find the right balance, whoever can be at their sharpest and fittest going into these first rounds of games, is going to like their chances."

Olsen indicated he wasn't particularly worried about dealing with the break, although he declined to specify which kind of scrimmage he would utilize. His thinking is that he's dealt with bye weeks so many times over the years that, "We all have a recipe for that."

Sure, he might change a few things here and there, but the concepts remain consistent, and he trusts his sports science department to get things right.

"There's a physical periodization, and there will be a tactical periodization from our side, but it's one that again has been, we've delivered, I don't know, 10, 15 times in the last three and a half years," he said.

Olsen admitted, though, that this time there's a twist.

"You're coming out of this into the most important game of the year, and that's a little bit new," he said.

Arena said he'll be going the intra-squad scrimmage route, although the international window brings another wrinkle to his preparations. What kind of condition will his four players that go away for international duty be in when they get back is a giant unknown.

"If you have players getting called up for international duty, they're likely starters in your team as well," Arena said. "So there's a lot of challenging things for coaches and players as you enter the playoffs. And this year it's been even more complicated because of the international window and the poor planning on the part of Major League Soccer."

This much is clear. Every manager will be trying to build momentum, wherever they can find it.

stories.headline: Dirk Kuyt leaves Fenerbahce a week after defeating Liverpool
stories.summary: Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.
stories.body:
ISTANBUL -- Dirk Kuyt left Fenerbahce on Wednesday, one week after guiding the team as interim coach to beat his old club Liverpool in the Champions League.

The former Netherlands forward took charge of that 3-2 win in Istanbul despite the club already having made a deal with Emre Belözoğlu to take over.

Kuyt returned in July to Fenerbahce, where he played from 2012-15, to assist coach Ismail Kartal who resigned last month.

"We thank you from the bottom of our hearts for all that you have contributed to these colors," Fenerbahce said in a social media post announcing Kuyt's exit. "Today we say goodbye to you but your place in this big family will never change."

Belözoğlu, a former captain of the club, takes over a team sixth in the Turkish league and 19th in the 36-team Champions League standings.

Fenerbahce's next Champions League opponent is Shakhtar Donetsk in London on Nov. 25.

stories.summary: The 2026 AFL draft is rapidly approaching, so here's your guide for what to know, including key dates and times, players to know, academy-linked names, and every club's pick.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is fast approaching. Marvel Stadium will once more play host to the first round at 7:00pm AEDT on November 19, with the draft recommencing for the second round onwards on November 20.

Key dates and times

West Coast: 3, 23, 56 (plus second round compensation pick)

Western Bulldogs: 42, 52, 53, 71

State of play and players to know
Essendon will be on the clock first, holding the top selection a decade on from the last time it took the number one pick to the AFL Draft. The Dons are expected to first bid on Port Adelaide-tied forward Dougie Cochrane, which will trigger a start-of-second-round compensation pick for the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles.

There are familial lines drawn throughout an exciting 2008-born cohort. Cody Walker is the son of high-flying Blue Andrew and will be headed to Princes Park. Cochrane is the son of former North Melbourne and Port Adelaide midfielder Stuart, though he isn't eligible to either team under the 100-game father-son rule. Instead, he's eligible to join the Power as part of their Next Generation Academy as an Indigenous prospect.

Top-10 riser Sam Gayfer is the nephew of 1990 premiership Pie Mick, and Koby LeCras brings goalkicking pedigree via 2018 premiership uncle Mark.

There will be up to five club-tied talents picked in the first round of the AFL Draft. But that won't necessarily result in an extended first night. Over the past five years the first round has averaged out to 25 selections accounting for father-son and academy bids, but clubs are expecting a number closer to the traditional 18 picks in the final intake of the 18-team competition.

Stricter stipulations around matching bids is at play, with clubs only able to use a maximum of two selections when matching for a club-tied prospect, meaning the selections of Port Adelaide, Carlton, Brisbane and GWS will be absorbed as early bids are matched.

We could see a record number of Indigenous talents picked in the first round. The high-water mark was four in 2005 and 2014, and all of Cochrane, Walker, Caylen Murray (Lions Academy), Toby Krasna and Jake Eime could be taken in the first round in 2026.

Thirteen of the top prospects have already been invited to Marvel Stadium on November 19.

Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody are all still in contention to be the open pool No. 1 pick, with Harry Van Hattum, Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris and Ethan Matthews (Giants Academy) rounding out the group on top of draft boards alongside Cochrane and Walker.

Murray, Gayfer, Wil Malady and Leo Steed have also received invites in a sign of club interest on night one.

Around 65 picks are expected to be taken across both nights which would surpass the 60 selections last year.

stories.headline: Qatar, Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as F1 rules out Imola backup plan for finale
stories.summary: Formula 1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a season-ending race, meaning the plan to finish 2026 in Qatar and Abh Dhabi is now set in stone.
stories.body:
Formula 1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a season-ending race, meaning the plan to finish 2026 in Qatar and Abh Dhabi is now set in stone barring unforeseen circumstances.

F1 had created a backup plan to finish the season in Italy on Dec. 6 in case hostilities resumed in the Middle East after the U.S. midterms.

The Italian circuit had started building grandstands but needed to know whether to commit to full-scale preparations.

On Tuesday, the deadline reported by ESPN last week, F1 has now let Imola know it will not be required.

It means as things stand, F1's season finishes with a triple header of races in Las Vegas on Nov. 21, Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.

Formula 1 has repeatedly stressed that it has been in constant communication with governments in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, while also monitoring travel advice from relevant European countries where the sport's 11 teams are based.

F1 was emboldened by the fact that MotoGP, also owned by Liberty Media, last weekend raced without issue in the Qatar circuit hosting F1 at the end of this month.

MotoGP team Yamaha pulled out of that event due to the company's global travel policy.

No F1 team has similar restrictions about travelling to the region.

The Imola news means F1 is full-speed ahead with its original schedule plan.

Sources have told ESPN that the final two races can still be scrapped if there were renewed hostilities in the Middle East.

Sources have confirmed in that instance, without Imola, that would mean the season ending with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

From a sporting context, both championships are settled -- Kimi Antonelli won the drivers' championship in Mexico, while Mercedes wrapped up the constructors' in Brazil. However, the constructors' championship is how teams are allocated their prize money and plenty of other teams are fighting for positions lower down.

Sources have told ESPN that F1's commercial agreement with the teams states there must be 22 races minimum in a calendar year, although their commercial agreements with broadcasters will be satisfied at the conclusion Las Vegas' event.

The U.S. and Israeli war in Iran earlier in the year forced F1 to cancel April races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, although Bahrain paid to reschedule with an event at Malaysian circuit in October.

Despite the rescheduled Bahrain race, were the final two races to be cancelled, F1 would be left with 21 races for the season.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: On the Munny: Cam's new role depends on Walsh groins
stories.summary: Cameron Munster is in a purple patch with his unlikely goalkicking heroics in this World Cup, but whether he continues in the final will depend on Reece Walsh's groins.
stories.body:
Cameron Munster is in a purple patch with his unlikely goalkicking heroics in this World Cup, but whether he continues in the final will depend on Reece Walsh's groins.

The Melbourne magician, a free agent since November 1, said his entire focus was on winning the World Cup and would not be drawn on his club future.

Sunday's final at Suncorp Stadium is expected to be a close contest with goalkicking possibly deciding the outcome, considering the Kiwis have the game's best marksman in Jamayne Isaako.

Munster has barely kicked for Melbourne in the past four years but has been nailing them like Hazem El Masri in his pomp with 11 goals from 15 shots with many of the attempts from the sideline.

He took over from Walsh in the 66-6 win over Cook Islands and continued in the 44-12 victory over Samoa in last week's semi-final.

With regular NRL goalkickers Sam Walker and Latrell Mitchell not in the starting side, the duties have fallen to Munster and he has done a great job despite admitting he does not practise.

"To be completely honest, I don't really like goalkicking," Munster grinned.

"I just do it because we've got no one in our squad doing it at the moment.

"Reece is our number one kicker, so if he feels good enough to do it on Sunday, he'll take over.

"If he pulls up a little bit lame on captain's run with his groins, I'll probably take over."

Munster had one of his best games this year in the semi-final win over Samoa where he ran the ball superbly and was a real handful.

His 18 runs was the most for any Kangaroo and throw in his 146m and three try assists it is a positive sign for the hosts.

"When I am playing my best, it is when I'm running the ball. That's the mindset and the aim for myself on Sunday," Munster said.

"The game might not be the same against New Zealand. I'm sure they've got a plan around myself and I'm sure I'll have to try and figure out a way to get around it."

Munster made his Test debut for Australia in the 2017 World Cup when he played two pool games at centre and halfback. He did not play in the 6-0 win over England in the final, but was No.6 in Australia's 30-10 triumph over Samoa in the 2022 World Cup final.

He has dared to dream about backing that up but said the process and not the outcome was on his mind as he attempts to enure the new players in the side get the satisfaction.

"I remember one of the boys, Jack Bostock, asked me the other day what it was like to win a cup," he said.

"It's something I've been very fortunate enough to be able to win, but these guys who have only just had their first World Cup, you try to give them that taste.

"You never know, four years' time, who's going to be able to be in the squad again."

Munster said in a previous interview he would delay travelling to Papua New Guinea until a later date after postponing a planned visit to talk to PNG Chiefs before November 1 that had been approved by the Storm.

Whether he will head to Port Moresby in future was not a subject he wanted to address on Wednesday.

"I am just focused on the World Cup," Munster said.

"My manager's dealing with all that sort of stuff and once the back end of this World Cup's done ... he'll sort that out, whether that's an option. If not, then it's not."

stories.headline: Kirk Cousins makes first comments on Minnesota trade at Great Clips
stories.summary: Kirk Cousins offered some thoughts on his trade to Minnesota after the news broke in the most on-brand location imaginable.
stories.body:
Before Kirk Cousins could head to the Land of 10,000 Lakes after being traded to the Minnesota Vikings, he had to make an on-brand stop: at Great Clips.

Cousins is a longtime aficionado of the budget-friendly salon chain, having been awarded its first-ever VIP card back in 2025 -- the "Hall of Fade" card affords free hair cuts to both Cousins and everyone who's at the location with him when it's used.

But it wasn't just a haircut for Cousins on Tuesday. When the veteran quarterback dropped by Great Clips following the trade, they took the time to get his thoughts on the news.

Reflecting on the trade, Cousins acknowledged that there was something in particular about the destination -- he quarterbacked the Vikings from 2018 to 2023 -- that made the transaction particularly special.

"There's so many memories, so many great people," Cousins said. "I understand the challenge on the football field, there's a lot of work to go get done, but it would be really special. If you're going to go win somewhere and have success, I want it to be in Minnesota."

He also had a message to Raiders supporters, complimenting the fanbase and organization for their hospitality in his short stay in Las Vegas.

"To the fans in Vegas, I just feel so grateful for how they welcomed me with open arms for the several months I was here -- that includes teammates, the organization," he said. "I really couldn't speak more highly of my time here in Vegas."

Cousins also addressed fans in Minnesota, saying he was excited to reunite with his former team -- though the roster wouldn't quite be the same as the one he left.

"To the fans in Minnesota, I'm thrilled to have the chance to come back," he said. "And to hopefully write the ending to a story for me that started eight, nine years ago when I first arrived. Ready to take on this new challenge with this, really, new team in Minnesota and see where we can go."

Asked for his parting thoughts before he left the hot seat (barber chair?), Cousins reflected on the balance between saying goodbye to his former team and also getting to reunite with a place he already had to depart.

"I've got a lot of emotions right now that are mixed. Always difficult to say goodbye, especially to people that mean a great deal to me, and there are so many of them here in Vegas," he said. "There's also a lot of people waiting for me in Minnesota that mean a great deal to me, that it was difficult to say goodbye to three years ago."

stories.headline: Sources: Man United contact U.S. Soccer over Poch; Carrick meeting Thursday
stories.summary: Manchester United have made contact with U.S. Soccer ahead of triggering Mauricio Pochettino's $10 million release clause as they close on a deal to hire the USMNT manager to replace Michael Carrick, sources told ESPN.
stories.body:
Manchester United have made contact with U.S. Soccer ahead of triggering Mauricio Pochettino's $10 million release clause as they close on a deal to hire the USMNT manager to replace Michael Carrick, sources told ESPN.

Sources added that executives from Man United are set to meet with Carrick on Thursday -- with the expectation that the 45-year-old will be relieved of his duties -- as the club pushes ahead with plans to hire Pochettino.

It will likely cost United another $2 million to hire Pochettino's staff, including long-time assistant Jesus Perez.

United executives including CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason WIlcox met with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday ahead of their Thursday meeting with Carrick.

Carrick signed a two-year contract in May, but has overseen a poor start to the season. United have won just one Premier League game -- against newly-promoted Ipswich in August -- and sit 18th in the table.

The club have so far remained tight-lipped about the future of former United star player Carrick, who was at Carrington on Wednesday to lead training with the players not currently on international duty.

Pochettino is preparing for two USMNT games against Haiti, one on Nov. 14 and another on Nov. 17, in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals.

A source told ESPN that U.S. Soccer said it expects Pochettino to oversee the two games against Haiti, the first for the Americans since winning all four matches during the Sept./Oct. international window.

Pochettino has extensive Premier League experience after spells at Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. He was considered for the United job before in 2018, 2022 and 2024.

United's next fixture is against Liverpool at Anfield on Nov. 22.

stories.headline: Senators' Cousins out 7-10 days after legal hit from Caps' Chychrun
stories.summary: Senators forward Nick Cousins will be out for a week to 10 days following a thunderous hit by Capitals defenseman Jakob Chychrun  that was ruled as legal during Tuesday night's game.
stories.body:
Ottawa Senators forward Nick Cousins will be out for a week to 10 days following a thunderous hit by Washington Capitals defenseman Jakob Chychrun that was ruled as legal during Tuesday night's game.

Senators' coach Travis Green said Wednesday that Cousins was knocked unconscious by the blow that sent him immediately to the ice late in the third period against the Capitals. Chychrun was not assessed a penalty for the hit following a review by on-ice officials, and ESPN's Emily Kaplan confirmed that the NHL's Department of Player Safety viewed the hit as completely legal and will not extend supplementary discipline toward Chychrun.

The Department of Player Safety believed Chychrun took a good angle, stayed low and drove through the body without reaching up or out toward the head.

There were three minutes remaining in regulation of Tuesday's game when Chychrun forcefully connected his left shoulder into Cousins' chest right when the forward's head was tilted away following a pass. Cousins' head subsequently hit off the glass and the ice when he landed. Cousins had to be helped off the ice and did not return afterward. Washington went on to win the game 3-2 in overtime.

In his postgame availability, Green said Cousins was "not doing great" but hadn't needed to be transported to the hospital. Green also didn't agree with the lack of action taken against Chychrun on the play.

"I'm a little surprised," Green said. "I thought it was a head shot to a player who wasn't ready for it. I guess they saw it differently."

Referees had originally called the hit a five-minute major penalty, believing Chychrun had connected directly with Cousins' head. After looking over the video, that was deemed not to be the case, removing the penalty entirely.

Chychrun had previously played in Ottawa during the 2023-24 campaign, before being traded to Washington.

stories.headline: Inside the tension, suspicion and history behind Amanda Nunes vs. Kayla Harrison
stories.summary: Kayla Harrison thought she had found a teammate, but Amanda Nunes saw a future rival. What really happened?
stories.body:
In their own ways, Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harrison both waited a very long time for what happened on June 7, 2025.

On that evening in Newark, New Jersey, Harrison submitted Julianna Peña to become UFC bantamweight champion. Nunes, who retired in 2023, was in attendance and eager to make a return to fight Harrison, with whom she shares a complicated past. The UFC allowed Nunes to enter the Octagon immediately after Harrison's win, so the two could square off on the spot.

That single encounter represented something Harrison had worked for her entire career: an opportunity to test herself against the very best. And even after two years away from competition, Nunes, considered the best women fighter in UFC history, remained that gold standard.

For Nunes, it was something else: a chance to expose a suspicion she'd held about Harrison for many years.

"I asked her, 'You planned this the whole time, right?'" Nunes told ESPN in January. "I wanted everybody to hear it from her own mouth. This is what was happening the whole time. You planned this."

Looking back, Harrison says she didn't understand at that moment the point Nunes was trying to make. The scene was chaotic. She had just fought, won a championship and was suddenly promoting her next fight. She managed to offer Nunes a simple response, "Let's do it," and only later understood the accusation being made.

"It didn't really sink in until I watched it later, and I was like, 'Oh, she really thinks I have been scheming this since the beginning," Harrison told ESPN on Nov. 3. "And to be fair, that would be a s---ty feeling. To think this whole time, your own team and coaches plotted against you. That is a terrible feeling that I can't even imagine.

"But it's just not true."

On Saturday, Harrison (19-1) and Nunes (23-5) will finally meet for the 135-pound championship at UFC 334 at New York's Madison Square Garden (Paramount, 9 p.m. ET), in one of the biggest fights in women's MMA history. Harrison is a two-time Olympic judo gold medalist and one of the most decorated combat sports athletes ever. Nunes is an icon of women's MMA, its greatest of all time. A two-division champion who overwhelmed such fighters as Ronda Rousey, Cris Cyborg and Holly Holm during her generational run at the top.

If that weren't enough, Harrison and Nunes have a history. They spent several years training at American Top Team in Coconut Creek, Florida. Harrison joined the gym in 2018, at the beginning of her MMA career. Nunes, who was already the UFC's dominant champion when Harrison arrived, left the gym in 2022, and eventually identified Harrison as her reason for leaving. In the time since, Nunes has accused Harrison -- and even others at American Top Team -- of planning this fight from the very beginning.

What unfolded between them could be described as deceit, misunderstanding or paranoia -- depending on who you ask. Both, Harrison and Nunes say that whatever the case, there's no animosity going into UFC 334. American Top Team owner Dan Lambert, for one, doesn't believe that.

"It's a hell of a story, and there's more between these two than they'll ever let us know," Lambert told ESPN in January. "They'll say all the right things about each other. But my opinion? They probably hate each other's f---ing guts is my opinion."

When Harrison first arrived at American Top Team, she was looking for a place to build her MMA career with others. She had spent her entire life in judo, and understood that reaching the highest level of even an individual sport, still requires a team. Including training partners.

She visited MMA gyms in New Jersey and Las Vegas before making her way to South Florida, where she instantly clicked with the coaches, the lifestyle and -- she thought -- one of the gym's prized athletes. Nunes.

"When I first met Amanda, she was like, 'Hey, you need to come here, it's great, I'd love to have you in camp,'" Harrison said. "And I was like, 'Oh, absolutely.' She seemed nice."

They sparred that week. Harrison was just starting out, and she remembers walking away from the session covered in bruises. They sparred only two rounds, Harrison said, but spending that time with Nunes felt good. Shortly after, she made a full commitment to American Top Team.

"It pisses me off thinking about it now, because I moved here with the expectation that we were going to be in it together," Harrison said. "I moved here thinking, 'Oh s---, we're about to level the f--- up. It's going to be me and her. And then obviously it ended up very different."

That expectation came from Harrison's experience in judo, where, she said, athletes regularly train with -- and then compete against -- each other. Harrison has memories of traveling through Hungary, Croatia and France, where she would work with women she might eventually face in the Olympics. For Harrison, there's no contradiction in that arrangement. Train together, improve together, and compete against each other if and when the time comes. She said she applies that mindset to her training now as a UFC champion, routinely welcoming and rolling with other bantamweights, including No. 15-ranked Bia Mesquita, at American Top Team.

"I don't have a scarcity mindset," Harrison said. "I don't think that for me to win, you have to lose. I think we all have our time and place and rising tides raise all ships."

Nunes views things differently.

She said she initially welcomed Harrison, but immediately picked up an energy that was different from regular work. Harrison wasn't there simply to innocently train alongside her. She was there to ultimately challenge Nunes in every sense of the word.

"I'm the kind of fighter who visualizes the future," Nunes said. "And from the first time I trained with Kayla, I told [my wife and then-UFC strawweight] Nina, 'I am going to fight this girl.' The first time we exchanged, I looked at Nina and said, 'This girl is different.'"

After that first spar, the two rarely worked together again. On this matter, at least, everyone agrees.

"How many rounds of sparring, real sparring, between them? Less than 10," American Top Team coach Mike Brown told ESPN in January. "Kayla always wanted to train with Amanda, but Amanda never wanted to train with her."

Nunes says she never interfered with Harrison's desire to join the gym and actually believes it was probably the right move for her career. But she maintains that Harrison should have been honest with Nunes, the coaches -- and herself -- on her reasons. "She didn't do anything wrong, wanting to come after me," Nunes said. "My life is all about the challenge. I love the challenge. I like that when you look at me, you want what I have. Let's go.

"But own it."

To be fair, in a very real way, Harrison did own it.

In 2018, before she'd even competed in MMA, she was already fielding questions about UFC titles, Nunes, Rousey and every other significant name at the top of the sport because of her undeniable potential as an Olympic gold medalist. And in all those interviews, she always said if the moment came that the challenge was Nunes, she would welcome it. That's what competitors do.

Nunes and those closest to her, however, saw it as one and the same. If Harrison's target was to be the best, and Nunes was the best -- then Nunes was the target. And there are certain realities to that in MMA.

"People talk like it's a high school wrestling tournament where you're like, 'Oh, I'm so happy for you,'" Nina Nunes told ESPN in January. "No. This is food in my kid's mouth. It's my kid's education. It's my legacy, forever. These are things that are very personal. It's fine if others don't see it that way. We see it that way."

In spite of the fundamental differences in which each viewed Harrison's presence in the gym, it managed to work for several years. Harrison signed with the PFL, and became the face of that MMA promotion. She won multiple tournaments, and twice signed exclusive contracts that prevented her from considering the UFC. The two champions of different organizations shared a facility and even coaches with one another, but did not cross paths -- in professional competition or even in training.

That all worked relatively well until December 2021.

On Dec. 11, 2021, Nunes was scheduled to make the sixth defense of her bantamweight championship against Peña at UFC 269 in Las Vegas.

Two months prior, Harrison had won her second lightweight championship in the PFL, and wrapped up her exclusive contract with the promotion. She began a period of free agency, in which she could field offers from other organizations, but the PFL maintained its right to match any in order to keep her in its roster.

Harrison, who had already fought four times in 2021 and was essentially out of the gym on holiday, flew to Las Vegas to watch her teammate, Nunes, defend her title.

"So, this is where it got a little weird," Brown said. "And you have to ask Dan [Lambert] about this, because he knows more about it than I do. But Amanda thought the UFC had plans that when she won, Kayla was going to get into the ring to challenge her. She believed there was some conspiracy to announce that fight."

When asked for his recollection of that event, Lambert gives a knowing smile but refuses to go into detail.

"I have a rule of never divulging s--- about what happens in the gym," Lambert says. "You have to ask Amanda. I'm not going to say what Amanda thought or what Amanda said, but one million percent, Kayla was not going to the UFC.

"I can even tell you that Kayla and her manager went to dinner with [UFC chief business officer] Hunter Campbell that week, and I told Hunter, 'No matter what happens at this dinner, no matter what happens at this dinner, I will kill [any potential deal]. I guarantee you, she is not going to the UFC [to fight].' I knew it would be a problem for Amanda, and there were other options for Kayla. There was an opportunity for Kayla to go make a bunch of money in Bellator MMA or PFL, and then go to the UFC a year later. That was my plan."

From Nunes and her family's perspective, all of it -- Harrison's backstage presence during fight week, her dinner with a UFC executive, an interview in which UFC CEO Dana White publicly confirmed his personal interest in Harrison -- was proof of what she'd felt, clearly, from Day 1.

She was always going to fight Kayla Harrison, and Kayla Harrison had always intended for it to happen.

"It was the biggest 'duh' moment of all time," Nina Nunes said. "She's a free agent. She's having dinner with the UFC. She's sitting in the front row.

"As much as they want to say, 'No, it's not what you think,' how could anyone think it was anything else? We didn't know if the UFC would bring Kayla into the ring, but we felt she was there for a reason."

At UFC 269 inside T-Mobile Arena, Nunes suffered one of the biggest upsets in UFC title fight history. As a more than 11-to-1 betting favorite, Nunes surrendered her bantamweight championship to Peña, tapping to a rear-naked choke at 3:26 of the second round.

Whether any of Nunes's performance that night can be tied to what happened behind the scenes is speculative. She has never publicly blamed American Top Team for the loss, which is her only defeat in 12 UFC championship fights. But by the time Nunes drove back to Florida from Las Vegas (she and Nina drive to the majority of her fights), she'd already decided to leave the gym and open her own facility in South Florida. Just like that, the 10-year relationship between Nunes and American Top Team, which had produced the greatest run in women's MMA history, was over.

Harrison found out secondhand.

"I was shocked," she said. "I had sent her a text when she lost, 'Let's get back in the gym and get this back,' and she'd responded something like, 'Thank you, cutie,' or whatever. And then the next thing you know, she was leaving.

"I couldn't understand it, because I've lost before, and it was on me. It wasn't on the coaches. The game plan wasn't flawed. I lost because I lost. And I felt that way about Amanda. She got in her own head that night. And that's on her."

The physical UFC belt that Nunes won for dethroning Cris Cyborg in December 2018 to become the only women's double champ is still displayed in the front lobby of American Top Team gym. But every photo of Nunes that once hung on the walls or rafters has been removed.

Lambert says he's long given up trying to make sense of athletes who come and go from his gym, but he won't celebrate them once they're gone.

"You're either with us or you're not," Lambert said. "You'll see pictures of [retired lightweight] Cole Miller up there with his American Top Team tattoos long after I die. But people who leave the gym? No.

"I'll keep her belt there, because that's testimony to what we did as a team, when we were together. I'm not putting a picture up and celebrating someone who didn't want to be here anymore."

Is the environment of American Top Team itself at fault for any of what happened between Nunes and Harrison?

Brown acknowledges that filling a practice mat with UFC contenders from the same weight class -- something that happens occasionally -- may not be the ideal training environment. As a coach, he encourages his athletes to push themselves, while also making their teammates improve. But he understand the potential conflict that approaches create.

"You don't want to be helping the guy next to you, giving him your secrets and your tricks, if you think he might be a future opponent," Brown said. "You're going to be selfish and keep everything to yourself. So, as a coach, I don't like the idea of pooling guys who might fight each other."

Lambert agrees, but doesn't see an alternative. As the gym's owner, his doors have always been open to the best talent in the world. There are certain realities that come with that, and it's up to the individual athletes to figure out what they're comfortable with.

"I've had issues where people at our gym have said, 'Hey, I don't want other people in my weight class in the gym,'" Lambert says. "And my response is always the same. 'How the f--- am I going to run a gym with one person in every weight class?' I could do that out of my garage. I want a gym that is full of killers in every weight class, because we think that's how people get better and get pushed between camps. We've had situations where teammates have had to fight. Sometimes they deal with it well, and sometimes they don't."

Both Nunes and Harrison adamantly deny Lambert's suggestion that they "hate each other's guts." They simply don't understand each other.

Nunes will never understand how Harrison and the team turned a blind eye to what she said was obvious from the very beginning. Harrison walked into her gym and challenged her place in the sport. She wasn't just open to the possibility of fighting Nunes, she wanted it. And eight years after they first met, the fight is finally happening. In Nunes' eyes, this was always the final destination, and she doesn't appreciate anyone -- least of all, Harrison -- who pretended otherwise.

Harrison, meanwhile, will never understand Nunes's lack of interest in what she initially offered: a teammate. Someone to push her, challenge her, and ultimately make her better. Harrison didn't go to Florida to take Nunes down, she said. She went to Florida so they could each become the best versions of themselves.

"Maybe the writing was on the wall for everyone, and I sound like the dumb blonde who didn't know we would eventually fight," Harrison says. "But she wasn't my goal. Of course, I wanted to get to the point where I was good enough to challenge her, but I was also just learning on the job and figuring things out."

They might never see the events of the last eight years the same way. But on Saturday in New York, they will settle the one question that might have been at the center all this time: Who is the best?

stories.headline: Ex-San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu files fair housing lawsuit
stories.summary: Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court.
stories.body:
Former San Diego FC forward Cédric Bakambu has filed a housing discrimination lawsuit in federal court against one real estate firm, two property owners and two real estate agents, according to information contained in the filing.

The lawsuit, a copy of which has been viewed by ESPN, alleges the defendants discriminated against Bakambu and his wife, Anne-Laure Hueber, on the basis of "familial status" by denying them the opportunity rent a house because they had children who would be living with them.

According to the lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California, the individuals and entities listed as defendants are property owners JW Wealth and Sheila Nasehi, real estate firm Compass California III and Compass agents Gillian Gillies and Bree Bornstein.

Neither Major League Soccer nor San Diego FC are named as a defendant in the lawsuit.

Bakambu and Hueber are seeking unspecified compensatory, statutory and punitive damages, as well as declaratory and injunctive relief, attorney's fees and costs under the Fair Housing Act, the California Fair Employment and Housing Act and the Unruh Civil Rights Act.

Bakambu signed with San Diego FC back on Sept. 3, and in nine matches for SDFC, he scored four goals with one assist.

In an Instagram post dated Nov. 6, Bakambu, a Congo DR international who played at last summer's World Cup, announced that he would no longer be playing for San Diego, stating, "Some decisions are beyond our control."

A request for comment from a representative for JW Wealth wasn't successful. A request for comment from Compass was also not successful.

ESPN has asked San Diego FC and the league for comment. the MLS players' association declined an ESPN request for comment.

The suit, which was filed on Monday, alleged two instances of discrimination. In the first alleged incident, Bakambu made an offer to rent a 5,679 square-foot house in San Diego, Calif. for a monthly rent of $17,500.

The filing details how Gillies, the agent representing Compass, stated that a pool barrier "would be required due to the age of the children" and asked whether Bakambu would pay an estimated $6,000 to install it if the owner approved.

Alternatives were proposed by Bakambu's broker, Sandra Shebani, including mesh covers and splash alarms.

Gillies responded: "A barrier will need to be installed."

The requirement wasn't mentioned in the property listing.

By Sept. 16, Bakambu made an updated offer that included paying a year's rent in advance, a Pool and Spa Liability Addendum, and an agreement to pay for the barrier.

According to the filing, Compass managing director Melanie Fontana later told Shebani that another applicant that met the lease requirements was under consideration, that Bakambu's offer had been received and that the owner would fund any pool safety measures.

The lawsuit goes on to state that on Sept. 18, 2026, Ms. Shebani raised the fair-housing concern directly with Kathy Mehringer, Compass's Broker of Record and Managing Director of Compliance and Risk Management.

Mehringer responded: "Melanie has explained the process. Compass is not violating any fair housing rules - why would you accuse us of doing so? That is not collaboration."

The filing states that Bakambu's offer was never accepted, and the rental listing was withdrawn from the market after his real estate agent raised fair-housing concerns with Compass management. The suit states that by tying rental conditions to the children and their ages, Bakambu and Hueber were discriminated against.

Later, Bakambu and Hueber sought to rent a 6,300 square-foot house through Compass in Rancho Santa Fe, Calif., and on Oct. 11, 2026, after viewing the property with Bornstein, offered a monthly rent of $23,500.

The filing states: "The offer and follow-up from Ms. Hueber went unanswered even after Plaintiffs observed the home being advertised for $20,000 per month by October 26, 2026."

On Nov. 6, the rental property was taken off the market.

The suit alleges that Compass and Bornstein, its listing agent for the second property, discriminated against Bakambu and Hueber by failing to consider or negotiate their offer because of familial status, and that this was in retaliation for Bakambu and Hueber raising fair-housing concerns regarding negotiations for the first property.

While this was going on, Bakambu's family was forced to remain in temporary housing at his own expense, according to the filing.

The filing reads: "Cédric and Anne allege that this sequence was not [an] ordinary rental negotiation. They were denied equal consideration because their household included five children, and Compass subjected them to further adverse treatment after they asserted their fair-housing rights.

"The consequences were concrete: lost housing opportunities, additional expenses, prolonged housing instability, disruption of efforts to arrange schooling and activities for their children, humiliation, and emotional distress."
